Story.p: Making Death World: Catachan characters is quick and easy. You should all create your first characters together at the beginning of your first session. Character creation is, just like play, a kind of conversation—everyone should be there for it.

You may need to make another character during play, if yours gets killed for example. On Catachan, death comes quickly and often. If so, no worries, the character creation process helps you make a new character that fits into the squad in just a few minutes. All characters, even replacement characters, start at first level.
Most everything you need to create a character you'll find on the character sheets. These steps will walk you through filling out a character sheet.

Look over the character specializations and choose one that interests you. To start with everyone chooses a different specialization; there aren't two snipers. If two people want the same specialization, talk it over like adults and compromise.

I sit down with Dan, Rob, Tom, and Kris to play a game run by Oli. I've got some cool ideas for a scout, so I mention that would be my first choice. No one else was thinking of playing one, so I take the scout character sheet.
All Catachan Jungle Fighters are human, but different regiments have different traditions and specialties. Choose your regiment. Your regiment gives you a special move.
I like the idea of being part of a regiment known for stealth—the Unseen Lurkers sound perfect. They wear dark fatigues and paint their wargear black, which fits my scout character perfectly.
Choose your character's name from the list.
Rock sounds good—tough and simple, like a Catachan should be.
Your look is your physical appearance. Choose one item from each list.

Hard eyes sound good since every Catachan has seen things that would break lesser men. No time for hair styling in the jungle so shorn hair it is. My fatigues are tattered and patched, covered in mud and blood from countless missions. Years of jungle survival have left me with a scarred body covered in the marks of close calls with death.

Assign these scores to your stats: 16, 15, 13, 12, 9, 8. Start by looking over the basic moves and the starting moves for your specialization. Pick out the move that interests you the most: something you'll be doing a lot, or something that you excel at. Put a 16 in the stat for that move. Look over the list again and pick out the next most important move to your character, maybe something that supports your first choice. Put your 15 in the stat for that move. Repeat this process for your remaining scores: 13, 12, 9, 8.

It looks like I need Wisdom to track and scout, which is my thing, so my 16 goes there. The defy danger option for Dexterity looks like something I might be doing to dive out of the way of a Catachan Devil's claws, so that gets my 15. A 13 Constitution will help me survive the jungle's many poisons and diseases. Intelligence might be useful in identifying threats and reading the signs, so I'll put my 12 there. Living is always nice, so I put my 9 in Strength for some extra damage. Charisma gets the 8—I'm not here to make friends, I'm here to survive.

Next you need to figure out the modifiers for your stats. The modifiers are what you use when a move says +DEX or +CHA. If you’re using the standard character sheets the modifiers are already listed with each score.
Your maximum HP is equal to your class’s base HP+Constitution score. You start with your maximum HP.
Base 4 plus 9 con gives me a whopping 13 HP.
The front side of each character sheet lists the starting moves. Some specializations, like the heavy weapons specialist, have choices to make as part of one of their moves. Make these choices now.

As a scout, I take the Hunt and Track move since that's what I do. I also take Camouflage since staying hidden is how I survive. I choose my signature weapon—a Catachan knife that's been with me through countless missions.

Your duty is a few words that describe what drives your character. Each specialization may only start with certain duties. Choose your duty—in play, it'll give your character certain actions that can earn you additional XP
The Survival option for scouts says I earn extra XP when I help the squad avoid a deadly threat. Rock is all about keeping everyone alive—I'll go with Survival.
Each specialization has choices to make for starting gear. Keep your load in mind—it limits how much you can easily carry. Make sure to total up your armor and note it on your character sheet.

I'm worried about my HP, so I take flak armor. My Catachan knife is my primary weapon, but I also take a lascarbine for ranged combat. It's a toss-up between the medkit and the antitoxin, but the medkit wins out since I'm the one who patches people up. I also end up with some rations and a canteen.

Now that you know who your character is, it's time to introduce them to everyone else. Wait until everyone's finished choosing their name. Then go around the table; when it's your turn, share your look, specialization and anything else pertinent about your character. You can share your duty now or keep it a secret if you prefer.

This is also the time for the GM to ask questions. The GM's questions should help establish the relationships between characters ("What do you think about that?") and draw the squad into the mission ("Does that mean you've served with Sergeant Jackson before?"). The GM should listen to everything in the description and ask about anything that stands out. Establish which regiment they're from, who they are, how they came together as a squad, or anything else that seems relevant or interesting.

"This is Rock, scout from the Catachan III 'Green Devils'! He's got hard eyes, shorn hair, tattered fatigues covered in mud and blood, and a scarred body. He's been on Catachan his whole life and knows the jungle better than most men know their own homes."

Once everyone has described their characters you can choose your bonds. You must fill in one bond but it's in your best interest to fill in more. For each blank fill in the name of one character. You can use the same character for more than one statement.

Take some time to discuss the bonds and let the GM ask questions about them as they come up. You'll want to go back and forth and make sure everyone is happy and comfortable with how the bonds have come out. Leave space to discover what each one might mean in play, too: don't pre-determine everything at the start. Once everyone's filled in their bonds read them out to the group. When a move has you roll+Bond you'll count the number of bonds you have with the character in question and add that to the roll.

With everyone introduced I choose which character to list in each bond, I have Dan's close combat specialist Marcus and Kris's medic Doc to choose from. The bond about saving someone's life sounds right, so I choose Marcus for it and end up with "Marcus owes me their life, whether they admit it or not." It seems like the scout and the medic work well together, so I add Kris's character and get "Doc has patched me up more times than I can count; I trust them with my life." I leave my last bond blank; I'll deal with it later. Once everyone is done I read my bonds aloud and we all discuss what this means about why we're together and what missions we've survived.

Take a little break: grab a drink, stretch your legs and let the GM brainstorm for a little bit about what they've learned about your characters. Once you're all ready, grab your dice and your sheet and get ready to face the jungle.
Once you're ready the GM will get things started as described in the First Session chapter.
